subject: falling person
title: Scientists Dropped People Off a Tower to Test If Fear Slows Time

scenes.text: Scientists dropped people off a 150-foot tower to find out if fear slows down time.
No rope. Volunteers fell backwards for about three seconds, hitting 70 miles an hour, into a net.
Strapped to each wrist was a screen flashing numbers just too fast to read.
If fear really put the brain in slow motion, they should have been able to read them on the way down.
They couldn't. Yet afterwards, they judged their own fall as 36 percent longer than everyone else's.
Time never slowed. A frightened brain just records more detail, and a richer memory feels like a longer one.

description:
To test whether time really slows down when you are terrified, scientists dropped volunteers off a 150-foot tower.
Neuroscientist David Eagleman and colleagues at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston used a thrill ride called SCAD, in which people fall backwards, with no rope, from a platform 150 feet up into a net, reaching about 70 miles an hour in a fall of roughly three seconds. Each volunteer wore a wrist display, a perceptual chronometer, that flickered numbers slightly too fast to read under normal conditions. If the brain sped up during the fall, the numbers should have become readable. They did not. But when asked afterwards, people estimated their own fall as about 36 percent longer than the falls they had watched. The team's explanation (PLoS ONE, 2007): in a frightening moment the amygdala lays down denser, richer memories, and an event remembered in more detail seems, looking back, to have lasted longer.
Has time ever seemed to slow down for you? Comment below.
first_comment: Their own fall felt a third longer than everyone else's, and it was the same fall. Has time ever seemed to slow down for you?
